common_name: Catesby's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Catesbaei, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Sarracenia x catesbaei is a naturally occurring hybrid between the purple pitcher plant (S. purpurea) and the yellow trumpet pitcher (S. flava), found wherever the two parent species grow together in the wild, combining the squat, wide-mouthed pitcher form of one parent with the tall, upright habit and yellow-green to red-veined coloring of the other in variable proportions. Like both parents it traps insects that slip down the waxy inner pitcher walls, supplying nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.

common_name: Moore's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia x Moorei, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Sarracenia x moorei is a naturally occurring hybrid between the yellow trumpet pitcher (S. flava) and the white-topped pitcher plant (S. leucophylla), combining the tall, upright, trumpet-shaped pitchers of one parent with striking white-and-red netted patterning on the pitcher hood inherited from the other. It is among the showiest of the naturally occurring Sarracenia hybrids and is sometimes seen in cultivation as a garden selection. As with other Sarracenia, insects are drawn to nectar at the pitcher rim, slip down the waxy inner walls, and are digested to supply nutrients. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.

As with other Sarracenia, insects are drawn to nectar at the pitcher rim, slip down the waxy inner walls, and are digested to supply nutrients the nutrient-poor bog soil cannot provide. common_name: Excellens Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia x Excellens, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Sarracenia x excellens is a naturally occurring hybrid between the white-topped pitcher plant (S. leucophylla) and the low-growing parrot pitcher plant (S. psittacina), producing pitchers with an intermediate form between the tall, upright, white-hooded pitchers of one parent and the squat, prostrate, curled-hood pitchers of the other. Where the parrot pitcher parent's influence dominates, plants may trap prey partly through a lobster-pot mechanism of inward-pointing hairs rather than a simple pitfall. As with other Sarracenia, give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.
